caption:
Why did artists protest the Eiffel Tower?

On 14 February 1887, the newspaper Le Temps published a petition titled "Artists against the Eiffel Tower." It was signed by a "Committee of Three Hundred" — one member for each metre of the planned tower — led by the architect Charles Garnier, and including Guy de Maupassant, Charles Gounod and Jules Massenet.

They called it "useless and monstrous," a "gigantic black smokestack" that would crush Notre Dame, the Louvre and the Arc de Triomphe under its "barbaric bulk." Garnier called it "a truly tragic street lamp." Alexandre Dumas called it an odious shadow.

The protest was already too late. The contract had been signed on 8 January 1887, and work on the foundations began on 28 January — weeks before the letter appeared. The minister Édouard Lockroy answered with mock praise for the petition's "beauty of its metaphors" and pointed out the project had been decided months earlier.

Garnier had sat on the commission that examined the proposals. He raised no objection there.

Eiffel answered by asking why something admirable in Egypt should become hideous in Paris. He then engraved the names of 72 French scientists, engineers and mathematicians onto the tower — chosen, the record says, precisely because of his concern over the artists' protest.

Some protesters changed their minds. Others did not. Maupassant supposedly ate lunch in the tower restaurant every day because it was the one place in Paris where the tower was not visible — a story the sources report only as hearsay.

Images: Louis-Émile Durandelle's construction view of November 1888; drawings from Gustave Eiffel's own office; an 1889 exposition poster; a photochrom of the finished tower; Bernardo Rico's 1889 engraving of the first platform; and Robert Delaunay's 1911 painting.
